newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-JACKIE ROBINSON'S FIRST SEASON ENDED IN TRIUMPH.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-JACKIE ROBINSON'S FIRST SEASON ENDED IN TRIUMPH.

text.p: When Jackie Robinson began his rookie season 50 years ago Tuesday, he was alone, viciously abused, and mired in a batting slump.
He ended it a hero to millions and a National League champion.
As he crossed major league baseball's colour line, his first problems were in his own Brooklyn clubhouse.
"There was a noticeable chill in the air when I first joined the Dodgers," Robinson, who died in 1972, remembered.

"A petition was written and signed by a number of the players requesting his nonemployment," recalled the late Dodgers' general manager Branch Rickey, architect of the "Great Experiment" bringing the first black into the big leagues.

It was a few Southerners on the team -- Dixie Walker, Bobby Bragan -- who tried to organise the move against Robinson, but South Carolinian Kirby Higbe reported it, and management stopped it. Pee Wee Reese from Kentucky was among the first teammates to welcome Robinson openly.
In Robinson's first appearances in a Dodger uniform in exhibition games against the Yankees, he did nothing special.
Then on April 15, 1947, his first official game, Robinson went hitless but had a key bunt that was mishandled to fuel a Dodger rally in a win over the Boston Braves at Ebbets Field.

In his second game, Robinson beat out a bunt -- the first of his 1,518 major league hits. The next day he hit the first of 137 career home runs. But soon he ran into a slump, going 0-for-20. He was under pressure like no other player ever.

On the Dodgers' first road trip, to Philadelphia, Phillies general manager Herb Pennock threatened a boycott, which Rickey quashed by saying he would accept a 9-0 forfeit. The Dodgers' usual hotel refused them because of Robinson. After a search, the club was accepted at the more expensive Warwick.

But the City of Brotherly Love had even worse in store -- the chorus of on-field abuse led by Phillies manager Ben Chapman. Dodgers travelling secretary Harold Parrott said that "at no time in my life have I ever heard racial venom and dugout filth to match the abuse that Ben sprayed on Robinson."
Robinson had promised Rickey he would "turn the other cheek" but the player, by nature a fighter, admitted later he came close to cracking.
In the third game in Philadelphia, Robinson's teammate Eddie Stanky finally yelled at the Phillies dugout to pick on someone who could fight back.
As Rickey had predicted, such incidents "built a surprising fight and stick-to-itiveness in team morale that lifted a club from that time into pennant contention."

In St. Louis, again there was a threat of a player strike, apparently with other teams involved and no objection from Cardinals maangement. But league president Ford Frick threatened to suspend anyone who joined.
Enos "Country" Slaughter spiked Robinson. Others would, too.
In his first 37 games, Robinson was hit by pitches six times. But knockdown pitches were not intimidating him, only bringing him back to his feet with greater fire in his eyes.

Cincinnati, a Ku Klux Klan hotbed, was another problem area for Robinson. The FBI took one of the many death threats against him seriously enough to search buildings surrounding the stadium. And Robinson's problems with hotels continued.

But the fans, black and white, were pouring into the ballparks to see Robinson, who was starting to hit, stealing wins with his speed and daring on the basepaths. One columnist called him baseball's most lucrative draw since Babe Ruth.
In May, he hit in 14 straight games. He had a 21-game streak in June, and the Dodgers pulled into first place for good in July.

A handful of other black players followed Robinson into the majors later in the season, most notably Larry Doby, signed by the Cleveland Indians on July 5 and quickly brought up as the first African-American in the American League.
Still, Robinson was leaving Ebbets Field by a secret exit, and every waking moment was a trial.
"Keeping myself in hand while I was playing ball was tough enough but I also had to be extra careful about my life outside of the ball park," he later wrote.

"While travelling with the club I was afraid to accept invitations to parties in strange towns or even to eat in a restaurant where I wasn't known. I worried about getting into a situation that would result in bad publicity. I was on guard night and day."

But Robinson was becoming known as the game's best player in pressure situations. He finished the season batting .297, 19th in the league, and wreaked havoc on the basepaths. He led the league with 29 stolen bases, was second in runs scored with 125 and bunted 42 times, 19 for hits.

In the Dodgers' pennant-clinching series against the Cardinals, he went 6-for-13 with a homer, double and four singles. Time magazine said "it was at least arguable that Jackie Robinson had furnished the margin of victory."

In late September, a triumphant parade proceeded to Brooklyn's Borough Hall, where it was announced Robinson had been named Rookie of the Year. September 27 was declared Jackie Robinson Day at Ebbets Field.
Robinson, fifth in voting for Most Valuable Player, was paid the minimum $5,000, but he and his teammates each earned $4,000 extra for making it to the World Series.
Although the Dodgers lost to the Yankees in seven games, Robinson would later help Brooklyn break through.
In Game 1 of the 1955 World Series, Robinson stole home -- his signature play -- and the Dodgers, losers of five previous Series to the Yankees, went on to their first championship.
Robinson, in later years a businessman and civil rights activist, retired after the 1956 season and was voted to the Hall of Fame in 1962. He died 10 years later at 53.
